caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was carved from a block of gypsum in 1868.

On October 16, 1869, two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, uncovered a ten-foot stone man. Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing. Three to five hundred people came a day.

The giant was made by George Hull, a New York tobacconist, after he lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about the giants of Genesis 6:4. With H. B. Martin he had a block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument. The block went to Chicago, where two sculptors carved it in Hull's own shape. Hull left off hair and beard after a geologist told him hair does not petrify. Pores were beaten in with steel knitting needles set in a board; sulphuric acid gave it age.

Geologist John F. Boynton said it was no fossil, guessing instead at a Jesuit carving. Andrew D. White of Cornell noted there was no reason to dig a well on that spot. Yale's Othniel Marsh saw fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum and called it "a most decided humbug." Hull confessed on December 10, 1869, and in February 1870 a court declared both his giant and P. T. Barnum's plaster copy fakes.

Still unresolved: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter, knew what he was making. And the copy in a Michigan arcade museum is Barnum's only because its owner says so.

Images: the giant photographed by Bain News Service, 1910; a Popular Graphic Arts lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant"; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry, held by the New York Public Library.

cards.headline: Carved in Chicago to <y>look like its maker</y>
cards.note: George Hull had the giant shaped after his own body. A geologist told him hair would not petrify, so the figure has none.

cards.note: Hull and H. B. Martin hired men at Fort Dodge in 1868 to cut a block ten feet four and a half inches long, telling them it was for a Lincoln monument.

cards.alt: Printed text on a pink card reading VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN, near Fort Dodge, Iowa.
